title: Temperance (ST II-II.141)
hookLine: moderation gives a kind of beauty to a life

lines: THE CHIPS STOP TASTING LIKE MUCH.
cards: Somewhere past the middle of a bag of chips, the chips stop tasting like much. The hand keeps going anyway. The pleasure left a while back, and the eating carried on without it.
Same with a show at one in the morning, or a phone in bed. Nobody decides to overdo it. It just keeps rolling.
Thomas Aquinas has a name for the virtue that catches that moment, and he says something odd about it. He doesn't call it grim, or strict. He calls it beautiful.

teach.h: THE PLEASURES CLOSEST TO THE BODY.
teach.b: For Thomas, temperance keeps a steady hand on the pleasures closest to the body: eating, drinking, and sex. These pull hardest, he says, because they're tied to keeping life going. Then the first surprise.
Thomas does not think less pleasure is always better.

teach.h: TOO LITTLE IS A VICE TOO.
teach.b: He names a vice on the other side, insensibility: refusing pleasure so far that you neglect what your body and life actually need. Despising a good meal is not, for him, a virtue. Temperance isn't hating pleasure.
It's enjoying it in the right measure. And the measure?
What life needs, and what fits your situation, your work, the people around you. A wedding feast and a Tuesday lunch have different measures, and both can be temperate. Now the second surprise.
Beauty belongs to temperance in a special way.

Beauty, for Thomas, has to do with clarity and right proportion. The pleasures temperance looks after are the ones that, left unchecked, cloud a person's reason, the very thing that lets a human life shine.
Temperance keeps that light on. So a temperate life isn't cramped. It's well-proportioned, like a room where nothing crowds out anything else.
The Book of Wisdom names it beside its sister virtues, in the Douay-Rheims: "she teacheth temperance, and prudence, and justice, and fortitude."
And Paul brings it to the kitchen table: "whether you eat or drink, or whatsoever else you do, do all to the glory of God." Eating isn't a distraction from God. It's one more place to give glory.

how: Catholics practice temperance in ordinary meals and drinks, and the Church sets days of fasting and abstinence, such as the Fridays of Lent; the Catechism teaches temperance as one of the cardinal virtues.

o: keeping a calm temper whenever you're angry
enjoying the body's pleasures in right measure
refusing pleasure as much as you possibly can

games.q: temperance, by Thomas — tap the pairs.
p: the vice of too little pleasure
what life needs and what fits

s: for Thomas, the less pleasure the better
he names a vice of too little, insensibility: refusing pleasure so far that you neglect what life needs.
beauty, for him, is clarity and proportion, and temperance keeps reason's light on.
the measure of temperance is the same for everyone, everywhere
Thomas says it's what life needs and what fits your situation. a feast and a Tuesday lunch differ.

games.q: a friend says the holiest thing is to take no pleasure in food at all. what would Thomas say?
o: agree: the less pleasure, the more virtue.
disagree: refusing what life needs is a vice too.
say pleasure doesn't matter either way.
games.why: Thomas calls it insensibility, a vice opposed to temperance. the virtue is the right measure, not the smallest one.

practice: Choose something small you can have now or soon, coffee or tea, a piece of fruit, a few squares of chocolate, and decide before you start how much is enough.

Take it slowly, actually taste it, and notice the moment the pleasure is full; stop there, without punishing yourself and without pushing past it. If you pray, give thanks for it, in your own words or a grace you already know.

wordCard.voice: Temperance. For Thomas, the virtue that enjoys the body's pleasures in the right measure: not too much, and not too little, which gives a life its proportion. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, the language Thomas wrote in: temperance, the virtue of the right measure.

carryVoice: Your line: enough is beautiful. The right measure gives a life its shape. Same time tomorrow.
